title: What Actually Is the Cloud?
sources: World Economic Forum, 'Why do we call it the cloud?' and Business Insider, 'This simple diagram explains why we call it cloud computing': engineers drew the internet / network as a cloud symbol in system diagrams, which gave cloud computing its name

AWS, 'Data protection in Amazon S3' (docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/DataDurability.html): S3 stores data redundantly across a minimum of three Availability Zones (separate data centers) so it survives the loss of a facility
Cloud storage = files stored on servers in data centers owned by a provider and reached over the internet (Google Cloud / AWS 'What is cloud storage?')

World Economic Forum, 'How does the internet cross the ocean?' and Engadget, 'How the Internet crosses oceans': the vast majority (about 95-99%) of intercontinental data travels through fibre-optic cables on the sea floor, not satellites

lines.text: When you back up a photo from your phone,
it doesn't float up into the sky.
It zips across the internet to a giant building,
packed with thousands of computers called servers.
And it gets copied to more than one building,
so if one goes down, your photo survives.
So the cloud is really just someone else's computer.
And the name? Engineers used to draw the internet
as a fluffy cloud on their diagrams.
But here's the twist: data crossing oceans
mostly travels through cables on the sea floor.
So the cloud lives on the ground, and under the sea.
lines.caps: SO THE *CLOUD | *LIVES | ON THE *GROUND | AND *UNDER | THE *SEA
